semantic_layer.text: Chapter 20: Current, Resistance, Ohm’s Law, Power, AC/DC

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: Hand-drawn simple circuit. A battery on the left is labeled V, with a pink plus sign at its upper terminal and a blue minus sign at its lower terminal. A black wire forms a rectangular loop. Blue arrows labeled I show conventional current moving clockwise: rightward across the top, downward along the right side, and leftward across the bottom. Black arrows and repeated e⁻ labels show electrons moving in the opposite, counterclockwise direction around the loop and downward through the battery.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Circuit diagram contrasting clockwise conventional current I with counterclockwise electron flow around a battery labeled V.

semantic_layer.text: Electrical current (I) is the rate of flow of positive charge.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t, which equals Q divided by t.

semantic_layer.text: It’s direction (from DC, or direct current, voltage) is opposite the ‘flow’ of electrons: from + to −.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The unit ampere equals coulombs per second.

semantic_layer.text: Example: A steady current of 2.5 A is created in a wire for 1.0 minute. How much charge passed by any given point, and how many electrons would this be?

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t, which leads to I equals 2.5 coulombs per second, equal to Q divided by t.
Q equals I times t, equal to 2.5 coulombs per second times 60 seconds, equal to 150 coulombs.
N equals 150 coulombs times one electron per 1.6 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs, equal to 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons.
n equals 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons times one divided by 6.022 times 10 to the 23 electrons per mole, equal to 0.0016 mole.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Unit: omega, ohm.
The units of ohms equal volts per ampere, equal joules per coulomb divided by coulombs per second.

semantic_layer.text: A resistor resists the flow of current. They’re often used to limit current in a part of a circuit. Wires themselves have some resistance, but we’ll usually ignore it.

semantic_layer.text: A flashlight bulb draws 300mA from its 1.5 V battery. What’s the resistance of the bulb? If the battery degrades and only produces 1.2 V how would the current change?

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Hand-drawn flashlight with a glowing bulb.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals V divided by R, so R equals V divided by I, which equals 1.5 volts divided by 0.30 amperes, or 5.0 ohms.
For V changing to 1.2 volts, I equals 1.2 volts divided by 5.0 ohms, which equals 0.24 amperes, or 240 milliamperes.

semantic_layer.text: Suppose you want to connect your stereo to remote speakers. (a) If each wire must be 20 m long, what diameter copper wire should you use to keep the resistance less than 0.10 Ω per wire? (b) If the current to each speaker is 4.0 A, what is the potential difference, or voltage drop, across each wire?

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: A stereo receiver connected to two remote speakers by separate copper-wire runs, each labeled 20 m.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Part b. Voltage equals current times resistance, which equals 4.0 amperes times 0.10 ohm. The voltage drop V sub R is 0.400 volt, or 400 millivolts.

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Circuit sketch of a voltage source connected in series to the resistance of the wiring and a speaker. Arrows labeled I indicate clockwise conventional current.

semantic_layer.normalized_math: \text{(a)}\quad \rho_{\mathrm{Cu}}=1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\!\cdot\!\mathrm{m},\quad L=20\,\mathrm{m},\quad R=0.10\,\Omega;\qquad A=\pi r^2=\pi\left(\frac d2\right)^2;\qquad R=\rho\frac LA=\frac{4\rho L}{\pi d^2};\qquad d^2>\frac{4\rho L}{\pi R}\Rightarrow d>\left[\frac{4\rho L}{\pi R}\right]^{1/2}=\left[\frac{4(1.68\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\!\cdot\!\mathrm{m})(20\,\mathrm{m})}{\pi(0.10\,\Omega)}\right]^{1/2}=2.1\,\mathrm{mm}
semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Part a. The resistivity of copper is 1.68 times 10 to the negative 8 ohm meters, the length is 20 meters, and the resistance is 0.10 ohm. Area equals pi r squared, or pi times d over 2 squared. Resistance equals rho L over A, which equals 4 rho L over pi d squared. Therefore d squared must exceed 4 rho L over pi R, so d must exceed the square root of that quantity. Substitution gives 2.1 millimeters.
Power equals energy divided by time.
Electrical energy U equals charge q times voltage V.
Power equals charge times voltage divided by time, which equals current times voltage.
Power equals current times voltage.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The unit ampere equals coulombs per second.
The unit volt equals joules per coulomb.
The unit watt equals joules per second.
The unit ohm equals volts per ampere, which equals volt-seconds per coulomb, which equals joule-seconds per coulomb squared.
Watts equal amperes times volts, equal coulombs per second times joules per coulomb, equal joules per second. Check mark.
From V equals I R, power equals I times I R, which equals I squared R.
From I equals V over R, power equals V over R times V, which equals V squared over R.
Power equals current times voltage.
Power equals current squared times resistance.
Power equals voltage squared over resistance.

V R M S equals the square root of the average of V naught squared times sine squared of omega t, which equals the square root of V naught squared times one half, which equals V naught divided by the square root of two.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance, implying current equals V naught divided by resistance times sine of omega t.

R M S current equals one over the square root of two times I naught.
Average power equals R M S current times R M S voltage.
Average power equals R M S current squared times resistance.
Average power equals R M S voltage squared divided by resistance.
